query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, the resistance to time‐dependent plastic deformation is primarily governed by the development of in‐situ interfacial barrier layers—such as thin oxide or compound films—that form at the interfaces between deposited layers and inhibit dislocation motion and diffusion‐mediated creep.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer coating composed of high-entropy alloy metal layers deposited under standard (ambient or low-oxidant) conditions.
generation.intervention: Expose the coating to high-temperature thermal aging (or cyclic thermal loading) in an oxidizing atmosphere to promote controlled formation of interfacial oxide/compound layers.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature conditions (e.g., 800–900 °C) under a sustained mechanical load that would normally drive creep deformation over time.
generation.structural_mediator: Continuous or semi-coherent interfacial oxide/compound layers that develop between the individual high-entropy alloy layers.
generation.mechanism: The formation of protective interfacial layers increases local residual compressive stresses and creates structural discontinuities that act as physical barriers to dislocation glide and diffusion. This reduces the rate of creep by limiting both the movement of defects and the diffusion of atoms necessary for time-dependent plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: When compared to coatings processed to suppress interfacial oxidation, the thermally aged (oxidized) multilayer coatings will exhibit a significantly lower creep strain over the same duration under identical mechanical loads.
generation.baseline: A similar high-entropy alloy multilayer coating fabricated under controlled inert conditions (preventing in-situ interfacial layer formation) that is known from prior work to exhibit conventional creep behavior.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective in environments where the temperature is high enough to trigger in-situ oxidation without causing overall coating degradation (e.g., between 800 °C and 900 °C) and under mechanical conditions where diffusion-assisted deformation is the dominant mechanism. In non-oxidative or lower-temperature environments, the protective effect may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The critical thickness, composition, and continuity of the interfacial barrier layers required to maximize creep resistance are not yet fully defined, and the influence of multilayer periodicity and processing parameters on these variables remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings: one set deposited under conditions that allow in-situ formation of interfacial oxide/compound layers by thermal aging in an oxidizing environment, and a control set fabricated under inert conditions that prevent oxide formation. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature (800–900 °C) mechanical loading for an extended period.
measurements: Record time-dependent plastic (creep) strain using high-temperature mechanical testing.
Perform electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) and XRD to assess the presence, continuity, and composition of the interfacial layers.
Measure residual stress distribution across the multilayers.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidized coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in creep strain (or fails to develop measurable and coherent interfacial barrier layers) compared to the inert-processed control coating, the hypothesis that interfacial barrier formation governs enhanced creep resistance is falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
